issues.subcategory: Operationalization mismatch: moral incongruence definition shifts between introduction and methods
issues.description: The introduction carefully defines moral incongruence as the statistical interaction of moral disapproval and behavioral frequency (disapproval × frequency). However, in the 'Present Study' section, the manuscript states: 'Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.' This substitutes 'severity of consequences' for 'behavioral frequency,' which is a fundamentally different construct. Severity of consequences is an outcome-adjacent variable and is likely endogenous to the addiction process itself, whereas frequency is an exposure variable. This definitional slip is never reconciled and would invalidate the core operationalization if implemented as written.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent Cohen's d conversions from effect size metrics
issues.description: The manuscript reports multiple effect sizes for the same studies with internally inconsistent conversions between metrics. For the smallest effect cited (Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020), the manuscript reports ΔR²=.012, f²=.016, Cohen's d=.22 in one location, then later reports the same study as ΔR²=.012, f²=.016, Cohen's d=.25. The conversion from f² to Cohen's d is d=2√(f²/(1-f²)) or via other formulas, but neither .22 nor .25 is consistently derivable from f²=.016 (which yields approximately d≈0.253 via d=2√f, or other values depending on formula). More critically, the two different d values (.22 and .25) are reported for what appears to be the same effect from the same study, creating an internal inconsistency that undermines the SESOI justification.
issues.quote: Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020).

issues.subcategory: SESOI defined in β units but equivalence test operates on different metric
issues.description: The authors set their SESOI as δ=|.11| described as a standardized β value, but then state 'Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region' using the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015). The Counsell & Cribbie test operates on standardized regression coefficients, but the equivalence region δ=.27 is stated separately from the β=.11 SESOI. The manuscript conflates two different SESOI values (.11 and .27) without clearly explaining which is operative for which test, creating ambiguity about what the actual equivalence bounds are. The δ=.27 appears in the analytic plan while β=.11 appears in the SESOI justification, and these are never reconciled.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11)

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent scale scoring for NIDA-ASSIST items
issues.description: The methods section states that the five NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items 'will be averaged.' However, three items use a 0–5 frequency scale while two items ('friend/family concern' and 'failure to control') use a 0/3/6 scale. Averaging items with fundamentally different response scales and ranges without standardization or transformation produces a composite score with unequal item weighting, where the 0/3/6 items contribute disproportionately to variance. This is a psychometric error that would distort the outcome variable. The supplemental materials confirm the 0/3/6 scoring for the latter two items.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months)... Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest.

issues.subcategory: Brief Pornography Screen scoring inconsistency between methods text and supplemental materials
issues.description: The methods section states the BPS uses 'a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' and that 'Responses are summed.' However, the supplemental materials show the BPS response options as Never (0), Occasionally (2), and Very Often (4)—a scale with values 0, 2, and 4, not 0, 1, and 2. This means the maximum possible score is 20 (not 10), and the scale is not a simple 0–2 scale as described in the text. This discrepancy between the methods description and the actual instrument would affect interpretation of scores and any benchmarking against validation studies.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt... by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: Problem Gambling Severity Index scoring inconsistency in supplemental materials
issues.description: The PGSI (Ferris & Wynne, 2001) is a validated instrument with a standard 4-point response scale of 0 (Never), 1 (Sometimes), 2 (Most of the time), 3 (Almost always), yielding scores from 0–27. However, the supplemental materials show response options of Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), Almost Always (5). This non-standard scoring (0, 2, 4, 5) deviates from the validated instrument, invalidates established cut-score interpretations (e.g., 0=non-problem, 1-2=low risk, 3-7=moderate risk, 8+=problem gambling), and introduces an irregular interval structure. The methods text states 'Responses will be averaged' rather than summed, which further departs from standard PGSI scoring.
issues.quote: problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index (Ferris & Wynne, 2001). This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: Pornography frequency scale anchor inconsistency between methods and supplemental materials
issues.description: The methods section states pornography viewing frequency will be assessed 'on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).' However, the supplemental materials show the scale anchored at Never (0) to More than Once Per Day (5), a 0–5 scale. Similarly, the ASSIST frequency scale is described as '0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)' in the substance use section but '1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)' in the pornography section. These inconsistencies suggest the scale anchors are not uniform across measures and the text descriptions are unreliable, which would affect centering, interpretation, and cross-behavior comparability.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: Oversampling of sports bettors creates non-comparable subgroups for gambling analyses
issues.description: The study combines a nationally representative sample (n=2,500) with an oversample of sports-wagering individuals (n=1,500). For gambling analyses, the effective N is listed as 3,325 (73% of national sample + 100% of oversample). However, sports bettors are a highly selected subgroup of gamblers with potentially different moral attitudes, frequency distributions, and problem gambling profiles than the general gambling population. Combining these groups without appropriate weighting or stratified analysis will produce a gambling sample that is systematically unrepresentative of the general population, biasing the moral incongruence interaction estimates for gambling specifically—the key comparison behavior. This is particularly problematic given that the study's central goal is to compare moral incongruence effects across behaviors.
issues.quote: Furthermore, due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically... Gambling | 73% (national sample) 100% (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: Inadequate power for key subgroup analyses with no pre-specified correction plan
issues.description: The power analysis reveals that prescription drug misuse (estimated n=140) has an estimated achieved power of only .301 for detecting f²=.015, and illicit substance use (n=240-480) has power of .472-.764. These are substantially underpowered for the primary equivalence tests. While the authors acknowledge this and propose an alternative equivalence region, the alternative region (lower bound of 95% CI for pornography β) is defined post-hoc relative to results not yet obtained, creating a circular dependency. Furthermore, the decision rule for when to switch analytic strategies is not fully pre-specified (e.g., what constitutes 'lacking sufficient power'), leaving researcher degrees of freedom in the choice of analytic approach.
issues.quote: in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small

issues.subcategory: Causal language used for cross-sectional correlational design
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, causal language is used to describe what are fundamentally cross-sectional, correlational associations. Phrases like 'moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction,' 'moral disapproval...amplifies the links,' and 'moral incongruence affecting well-being' imply directional causation. The proposed study is explicitly cross-sectional (acknowledged in limitations), meaning temporal ordering cannot be established. It is equally plausible that feeling addicted leads to moral disapproval (reverse causation), or that a third variable (e.g., neuroticism, religiosity) drives both. The limitations section acknowledges cross-sectionality but the framing throughout the paper does not adequately hedge causal claims.
issues.quote: moral disapproval of pornography likely amplifies the links between pornography use and self-reported feelings of compulsivity or addiction... moral incongruence affecting well-being... moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction

issues.subcategory: Reverse causation not addressed for moral disapproval as outcome vs. predictor
issues.description: The moral incongruence model treats moral disapproval as a predictor of self-reported addiction feelings. However, it is theoretically plausible—and empirically supported in stigma literature—that experiencing problems with a behavior leads individuals to morally condemn that behavior post-hoc as a self-justification or shame response. The manuscript briefly acknowledges that 'disapproval of and distress regarding one's own behaviors are likely related to each other' but dismisses this as a reason to use the interaction term rather than treating it as a fundamental threat to the causal model. No instrumental variable approach, lagged design, or other causal identification strategy is proposed.
issues.quote: Another plausible, if not likely, explanation is that disapproval of and distress regarding one's own behaviors are likely related to each other. More simply, it is not surprising to find links between these two domains as they are both negatively valenced judgments about the same behavior.

issues.subcategory: Moral disapproval measured for all participants regardless of behavior engagement, creating conceptual mismatch
issues.description: The methods state that 'key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior.' This means moral disapproval of pornography will be assessed even among non-users, and the interaction term (disapproval × frequency) will be computed for non-users where frequency=0. Including non-users in the moral incongruence interaction fundamentally changes the construct being measured: for non-users, the interaction term is zero by definition regardless of disapproval level, which will attenuate the interaction effect and conflate non-use-due-to-disapproval with use-despite-disapproval. The original PPMI model was explicitly developed for users only.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.subcategory: Single-item moral disapproval measure lacks validation and may conflate distinct constructs
issues.description: Moral disapproval for all substances and behaviors is assessed with a single item ('I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'). Single-item measures have well-documented reliability limitations, and moral attitudes toward behaviors are multidimensional (e.g., harm-based vs. purity-based moral concerns, personal vs. societal moral judgments). The manuscript acknowledges this measure is 'not currently validated for gambling or pornography' in the context of the ASSIST but does not acknowledge the broader psychometric limitations of single-item moral disapproval measures. No test-retest reliability or convergent validity data are cited for these items.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency operationalized as average across gambling types rather than overall frequency
issues.description: The methods state 'To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.' However, the supplemental materials show only a single gambling frequency item ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). It is unclear what multiple gambling behaviors are being averaged, as only one item appears in the supplemental instrument. If only one item is used, averaging is meaningless. If multiple items exist but are not shown, this represents a reporting completeness gap. Furthermore, averaging frequency across different gambling types (e.g., daily lottery vs. monthly casino) conflates very different behavioral patterns.
issues.quote: To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: Pornography measure assesses only solitary use, excluding partnered pornography use
issues.description: The supplemental materials show that pornography viewing frequency is assessed only for 'Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner).' This operationalization excludes partnered pornography use, which is a distinct behavioral pattern with different correlates and moral valence. The BPS and moral disapproval items do not make this distinction. This creates a mismatch between the frequency predictor (solo use only) and the outcome/disapproval measures (pornography use generally), potentially attenuating the interaction effect for pornography relative to other behaviors where no such restriction exists.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: No control for multiple comparisons across eight simultaneous moderation analyses
issues.description: The study proposes eight moderation analyses (pornography, gambling, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, and an eighth implied by the count in the analytic plan) with no pre-specified correction for familywise error rate. While the authors mention 'Holm-adjusted test statistics' for bivariate correlations, no such correction is described for the primary moderation analyses. With eight tests at α=.05, the probability of at least one false positive is approximately 34%. This is particularly problematic given that the study's confirmatory hypothesis for pornography (expecting a significant interaction) and null hypotheses for other behaviors could be spuriously supported or refuted due to Type I or Type II errors without appropriate correction.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: Exploratory fallback analyses not fully pre-specified, creating researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The manuscript describes multiple contingent analytic strategies: (1) if OLS assumptions are violated, 'supplemental analyses' will be conducted with unspecified methods; (2) if moral incongruence for gambling/substances exceeds the equivalence region, 'exploratory analyses' will redefine the equivalence region using the lower bound of the pornography CI; (3) for underpowered subgroups, an alternative equivalence region will be used. None of these fallback procedures are fully pre-specified (e.g., which alternative regression technique will be used for assumption violations, exact decision thresholds for switching strategies). This creates substantial researcher degrees of freedom that undermine the registered report format.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate... In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence

issues.subcategory: Centering procedure for interaction terms inconsistently described
issues.description: The analytic plan states that 'focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated' in SPSS. However, it later states 'For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.' These two statements are contradictory: one specifies centering before computing the product (standard practice for reducing multicollinearity in moderation), while the other specifies using raw (uncentered) values. This ambiguity means the actual analytic procedure is underspecified and the two approaches will yield different interaction terms and potentially different results.
issues.quote: focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated... For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: Missing pre-registration details: registry, date, and access information
issues.description: Despite being described as a 'Registered Report,' the manuscript does not specify where the study is pre-registered, the registration date, the registration number, or a URL to access the registration. For a registered report, this information is essential for verifying that the hypotheses and analytic plan were committed to prior to data collection. The absence of this information makes it impossible to verify the integrity of the registered report format.
issues.quote: Moral Incongruence and Addiction: A Registered Report

issues.subcategory: Covariates assessed via panel data not described in sufficient detail for replication
issues.description: Age, gender, and religiousness are described as being 'assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey).' While the religiousness items are described, the exact operationalization of age (continuous? categorical?) and gender (binary? how many categories? how non-binary individuals are handled?) are not specified. The analytic plan specifies 'gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male)' which collapses all non-male genders into a single category without justification or acknowledgment of this limitation. This is both a reporting gap and a potential construct validity issue.
issues.quote: Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey)... gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: Missing description of how the sports-wagering oversample was recruited and screened
issues.description: The manuscript states that 1,500 adults with 'recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically' will be recruited, but provides no details about how this group will be identified, screened, or verified. It is unclear whether self-report of past-year sports wagering is sufficient, what the screening question is, whether there is a minimum frequency threshold, or how YouGov will identify this population. This information is essential for evaluating the representativeness and composition of this oversample.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

issues.subcategory: Unrealistic assumption of zero missing data without justification
issues.description: The manuscript states 'we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data' and 'we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles.' This assumption is unrealistic for any survey study, even with professional panel providers. No missing data handling strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation, full information maximum likelihood) is specified. In a study with sensitive topics (pornography use, substance use, gambling), item non-response is particularly likely. The absence of a missing data plan is a significant methodological gap for a registered report.
issues.quote: we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: Overclaim that findings will generalize to 'addictions broadly' from a non-clinical sample
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames its goal as understanding 'addictions broadly' and draws implications for clinical diagnosis (CSBD criteria, ICD-11). However, the sample is a general population/community sample, not a clinical sample. The authors acknowledge in limitations that 'the effects of moral incongruence on feelings of addiction are most critical in treatment seeking populations' and that 'prevalence rates in clinical settings are largely unknown.' Despite this acknowledgment, the framing throughout the paper implies that findings will directly inform clinical diagnostic practice, which is an overclaim given the non-clinical sample.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only sample limits generalizability given known cultural variation in moral incongruence effects
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that 'moral incongruence as it relates to pornography use does appear to vary somewhat by the cultural context in which it is studied' and cites studies from Poland, Croatia, and Germany showing different effect sizes. Despite this, the study uses only a U.S. sample and draws broad conclusions about whether moral incongruence is 'unique to sexual behavior' as a general principle. The U.S. has a particularly high prevalence of religious conservatism compared to many Western nations, which may inflate moral incongruence effects for pornography relative to other behaviors in ways that would not replicate cross-culturally.
issues.quote: Although a nationally representative sample in the U.S. is better than convenience sampling methods, such a sample represents only one broad cultural context in which these hypotheses could be tested. Given that moral incongruence as it relates to pornography use does appear to vary somewhat by the cultural context in which it is studied

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis directionality for gambling moral disapproval main effect contradicts null interaction hypothesis
issues.description: The authors hypothesize (Hypothesis 2a) that 'moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems' as a main effect, while simultaneously hypothesizing (Hypothesis 2b) that the interaction of moral disapproval and gambling frequency will be null. However, if moral disapproval predicts gambling problems as a main effect, this implies that disapproval affects problem perception independently of frequency—which is itself a form of moral incongruence effect (the original, pre-revised PPMI conceptualization). The theoretical framework does not adequately explain why a main effect of disapproval would exist for gambling but the interaction would not, given that the revised model explicitly moved away from main effects toward interactions as the proper operationalization of moral incongruence.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems, even when including gambling frequency, religiousness, gender, and age as covariates in a regression model. However, we do not expect to find that the interaction of moral disapproval of gambling and gambling frequency will significantly predict self-reported gambling disorder symptoms.

issues.subcategory: Confirmation bias in hypothesis framing: study designed to confirm uniqueness of pornography effect
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states 'we aim to demonstrate that...the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior' and 'a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.' This framing reveals a confirmatory rather than exploratory orientation that is at odds with the registered report format, which is designed to reduce confirmation bias. The hypotheses are structured so that the 'expected' outcome (pornography unique, others null) aligns with the authors' theoretical commitments and the interests of the funding body (International Center for Responsible Gaming, which has an interest in gambling not being seen as uniquely morally problematic).
issues.quote: we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study... with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors... Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior

issues.subcategory: Potential conflict of interest: funder has stake in gambling-specific findings
issues.description: The study is funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming (ICRG), an organization with interests in the gambling industry. The study is designed to test whether moral incongruence is unique to pornography/sexual behavior and not present for gambling. A finding that gambling is not subject to moral incongruence effects would be favorable to the gambling industry by suggesting that self-reported gambling problems reflect genuine disorder rather than moral bias. No conflict of interest statement is included in the manuscript, and the potential influence of funder interests on hypothesis framing is not acknowledged.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming.

issues.subcategory: Alcohol frequency measure inconsistency: general use vs. heavy episodic drinking
issues.description: The methods describe a modification to the NIDA Quick Screen for alcohol: 'for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).' However, the supplemental materials show that the gender-specific heavy drinking questions (4+ drinks for women, 5+ drinks for men) are also included. It is unclear whether the general alcohol frequency item or the heavy drinking items will be used as the 'frequency' predictor in the moral incongruence interaction, or how these will be combined. General alcohol consumption frequency and heavy episodic drinking are distinct constructs with different relationships to alcohol use disorder.
issues.quote: for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed). Although we will include these response options

issues.subcategory: Non-tobacco nicotine and tobacco products collapsed into single frequency item despite different addiction profiles
issues.description: The study collapses smoked tobacco, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco into a single frequency item. These products have substantially different addiction profiles, health consequences, social stigma, and moral valence. A daily cigarette smoker and an occasional vape user would receive the same frequency score despite very different behavioral patterns. This aggregation reduces construct validity for the nicotine/tobacco frequency measure and may obscure differential moral incongruence effects across nicotine delivery methods.
issues.quote: we will include specific mention of non-cigarette nicotine products alongside of tobacco products. That is, we will make it explicitly clear that smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine.

issues.subcategory: NIDA-ASSIST not validated for pornography or gambling use as outcome measures
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that including pornography and gambling in the NIDA-ASSIST 'is not currently validated for gambling or pornography' but argue this 'will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses' because validated scales are also included. However, the NIDA-ASSIST items for pornography and gambling will be used as outcome variables in the primary analyses (Table 1 shows ASSIST items as the measure for all substances, and as one of two measures for pornography and gambling). Using unvalidated adaptations of a substance use screening tool for behavioral outcomes introduces unknown measurement error and may produce systematically biased estimates.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction between 'all participants complete all measures' and 'only past-year users complete further measures'
issues.description: The methods contain a direct contradiction regarding who completes which measures. In the substance use section, it states 'Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.' In the pornography section, it states 'only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months...will complete the remaining items.' However, the data screening section states 'key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.' These statements are mutually contradictory and it is unclear which procedure will actually be followed.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use... key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.subcategory: Discrepancy in effect size reporting for Grubbs, Kraus et al. (2020) across manuscript sections
issues.description: The manuscript cites Grubbs, Kraus, et al. (2020) with different effect sizes in different sections. In the analytic plan, it reports 'β = .27, 95% CI [.23, .31], ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69' for one sample from this study. Earlier in the analytic plan, it reports 'ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24' and 'ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69' and 'ΔR2 = .12, f2 = .23, Cohen's d = .97' all attributed to Grubbs, Kraus, et al. (2020). While these may represent different samples within the same paper, this is not clearly explained, and the conversion from f2=.12 to Cohen's d=.69 and from f2=.23 to Cohen's d=.97 are not consistent with standard conversion formulas (f2=.12 → d≈0.69 is approximately correct via d=2√f2 only if f2 is interpreted as η², suggesting metric confusion).
issues.quote: small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020)... to moderate (ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020), to relatively large (ΔR2 = .12, f2 = .23, Cohen's d = .97, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: No description of how the interaction term will be interpreted or probed
issues.description: While the manuscript describes using the Interactive Shiny application to visualize interactions, it does not specify how significant interactions will be probed (e.g., simple slopes at ±1 SD, Johnson-Neyman regions of significance, floodlight analysis). For the primary hypothesis that moral disapproval moderates the frequency-addiction relationship, the direction and pattern of the interaction (not just its significance) is theoretically critical. The manuscript does not pre-specify what pattern of results would constitute support for the moral incongruence hypothesis versus alternative patterns (e.g., crossover interactions, ordinal interactions).
issues.quote: To visualize results, consistent with prior works on moral incongruence (Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020), we will make use of the Interactive Shiny application (McCabe et al., 2018). Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates of the outcome.

issues.subcategory: Flora & Curran (2004) cited in references but never mentioned in text
issues.description: The reference list includes Flora, D. B., & Curran, P. J. (2004), a paper on estimation methods for confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data. This reference does not appear to be cited anywhere in the manuscript text. Its presence in the reference list without a corresponding in-text citation suggests either a missing analysis (e.g., a planned CFA that was removed from the methods) or a copy-paste error from another manuscript. If a CFA was planned and removed, this represents an undisclosed analytic decision.
issues.quote: Flora, D. B., & Curran, P. J. (2004). An empirical evaluation of alternative methods of estimation for confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data. Psychological Methods, 9(4), 466–491.

issues.subcategory: Rosseel (2012) lavaan citation in references but not cited in text
issues.description: The reference list includes Rosseel, Y. (2012) for the lavaan R package, which is used for structural equation modeling. This package is not mentioned anywhere in the manuscript text, and no SEM analyses are described in the analytic plan. Like the Flora & Curran citation, this suggests either a planned analysis that was removed without updating the reference list, or a copy-paste error. If SEM was originally planned, its removal without explanation represents an undisclosed analytic decision.
issues.quote: Rosseel, Y. (2012). lavaan: An R package for structural equation modeling and more Version 0.5-12 (BETA). Journal of Statistical Software, 42, 1–36.

issues.subcategory: No blinding or separation between primary study purpose and focal measures
issues.description: Participants are recruited for 'a larger study of sports wagering behaviors' but will also complete measures of pornography use, moral disapproval of various behaviors, and addiction symptoms. The primary framing of the study (sports wagering) may create demand characteristics or response biases when participants encounter questions about pornography and moral disapproval. Participants who self-identify as sports bettors may respond differently to moral disapproval questions about gambling than they would in a neutral context. No attention to this potential framing effect is discussed.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming. The primary focus of this project is to assess the prevalence of sports-wagering behaviors in the American public

issues.subcategory: Temporal mismatch between outcome measures: BPS uses 6-month window, ASSIST uses 3-month window, frequency uses 12-month window
issues.description: The study uses three different time windows across its key measures: the Brief Pornography Screen asks about 'the last 6 months,' the NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items ask about 'the past three months,' and the frequency measures ask about 'the past 12 months.' These temporal mismatches mean that the predictor (12-month frequency) and outcomes (3-month or 6-month problems) cover different time periods, reducing the conceptual coherence of the regression models and potentially attenuating associations. This is particularly problematic for the parallel analysis goal, as pornography uses the 6-month BPS while substances use the 3-month ASSIST.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, 'In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?'... 'In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?'... 'In the past 12 months, how often have you used the following?'
